corrections.baseline: zlib-ng and zstd software compression (Intel RocksDB guide); Snappy and CPU deflate execution in DuckDB (ADMS 2025 paper)
corrections.claimed_speedup: Snippet only, no page opened. ADMS 2025 paper ('A Hot Take on the Intel Analytics Accelerator for Database Management Systems') per search snippet: DuckDB Deflate on IAA reaches 4.59 GB/s compression and 18.24 GB/s decompression; up to 10x faster decompression than DuckDB's Snappy in microbenchmarks and up to 30% lower end-to-end TPC-H query latency. Intel RocksDB tuning guide per search snippet: 103% higher throughput and 64% lower p99 latency than zstd for an 80:20 read/write mix with 16KB blocks and 256B values (this differs from the 34%-95% / 23%-51% range in the original record; neither could be checked against the page). The zlib-ng figures (92%-205% throughput, 53%-74% p99) were not confirmed by any snippet this verifier saw.
corrections.caveats: Hardware-gated: the speedups come from the Intel IAA accelerator on 4th-gen Xeon (Sapphire Rapids) and later, a different machine class from a software codec; QPL's software fallback path has no published comparison against zlib-ng or zstd. Every number is snippet only: intel.com, vldb.org and cs.cmu.edu were EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the paper and guide were not opened. Intel guide is vendor-run (tier C at best); the RocksDB result runs through Intel's separate IAA RocksDB plugin built on QPL. The repo's own benchmark framework (tools/benchmarks, google-benchmark based) reports IAA throughput only, e.g. about 1.26-1.76 GB/s per job in the quick-start sample output, with no baseline. Retier candidate: open the ADMS 2025 paper for a peer-reviewed tier B check.

tier_reason: First-party README table and pareto_graph.png compare LZSA against LZ4/LZ4_HC on ratio (Silesia, Canterbury, Calgary, enwik9) and on ZX Spectrum (Z80) decompression rate; no compiler, flags or host CPU and no benchmark harness, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README table 'Decompression speed vs. LZ4' (ZX Spectrum/C64 file set): LZSA1 90%, LZSA2 75%, LZ4_HC -19 -B4 -BD 100%, i.e. slower than LZ4 at default settings. The README's pareto_graph.png (ZX Spectrum, decompression rate in bytes per frame) plots the fastest LZSA1 variants (LZSA1-m4, LZSA1-m5) at about 2,400-2,570 bytes/frame against about 2,170-2,360 for the two LZ4 decompressors, roughly 9% faster at the top end (derived from page data, read off the graph, approximate), while also compressing better. Compression ratio beats LZ4_HC -19 on every listed corpus, e.g. Silesia LZSA1 34.78% and LZSA2 32.52% versus LZ4_HC 36.47%; enwik9 35.54% / 33.49% versus 37.18%. The README also says the compressor is about 2x slower than LZ4_HC.
corrections.caveats: The speed win exists only for 8-bit decompressors (Z80 graph) and only for the speed-tuned LZSA1 modes; the README's own table reads slower than LZ4 on decompression (90% and 75%), and the compressor is about 2x slower than LZ4_HC, so on modern CPUs this is a ratio win, not a speed win. No host CPU, compiler, flags or benchmark harness; the graph values are approximate readings. Licensing is mixed but all OSI/CC0: Zlib for the code, CC0 for src/matchfinder.c (no patent grant for that file). Last commit 2023-02-27, over 3 years old.

notes: Pareto graph shows LZSA1-m4/m5 beating LZ4 on Z80 decompression speed, so the 'faster than LZ4 on 8-bit' prose has numbers behind it (graph only); not faster on any axis on modern hosts. Metadata confirmed: 261 stars, not archived, not a fork, last commit 2023-02-27 (abandoned).
